catalog_locator: Chapter 2 Phonology, section 2.9 'Stress', p. 219 (= PDF page 233 of PL-557), examples (2.66)-(2.67); tone: section 2.7-2.7.1, pp. 215-218; word length: section 2.8.2; compound stress: ch. 3, p. 224. Saved file: the copy we hold (text layer; page 233 re-rendered at 300 dpi and read as an image by the third reader).
catalog_quote: Stress in Sherpa falls on either the first or the second syllable in disyllabics, although initial stress is more frequent. For example: (2.66) 'lúŋ.ba 'village'; 'zím.bu 'grab'; 'ʈhì.muŋ 'ankle'; ór.'tuk 'gale'; sà.'šiŋ 'field'; mà.'yaŋ 'family'. I have not, as yet, been able to work out a clear patterning for stress placement; the distribution may be lexically determined. Initial and non-initial stress both occur with high and low tone words, with the full array of vowels in the nucleus of the stressed syllable, (excepting the low back vowel /ɑ/ which occurs only in unstressed syllables) and with the full inventory of possible consonants in syllable onsets. The patterning in polysyllabic words is clearer, as stress falls on the penultimate syllable, however there are few polysyllabic words in the database. For example: (2.67) lò.ti.'di.yu 'satisfy'; bù.'gyel.daŋ 'worm'.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Sherpa (sher1255) is not in the catalog. Both title-hit items are non-contributing: Green & Tobin 2009 is an autism-prosody clinical paper mis-linked to xsr by Glottolog's computerised assignment (not relevant, not downloaded, DOI 10.1080/17549500903003060); Pittman 1970 (read from the archive.org scanned of ERIC ED046002 already held by the project) is a register/tone comparison that reports Gordon's Sherpa pitch patterns on noun+-ki phrases and says nothing about word-stress placement in Sherpa. The only explicit stress statement found is Kelly 2004 (Pacific Linguistics 557, open CC BY-SA), section 2.9 p. 219: disyllables stress first or second syllable with no clear rule (initial more frequent, possibly lexical, independent of tone), penultimate in polysyllables. Gordon's 1970 'Sherpa phonemic summary' (Hale & Pike Part I, ERIC ED046001, pp. 45-60) would be the most likely older primary source but ERIC shows 'PDF pending restoration' and no archive.org copy exists; Rosetta Project xsr items are only Gordon's interlinear texts (downloaded, no stress content). new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (ANU open-access PL-557, CC BY-SA), printed p. 219 = PDF page 233, rendered to an image and read directly; text layer lines 1429-1449. Kelly 2004, ch. 2 Phonology, section 2.9 'Stress' is exactly as quoted: 'Stress in Sherpa falls on either the first or the second syllable in disyllabics, although initial stress is more frequent' (ex. 2.66 'lung.ba, 'zim.bu, 'thi.mung vs or.'tuk, sa.'sing, ma.'yang); 'I have not, as yet, been able to work out a clear patterning for stress placement; the distribution may be lexically determined. Initial and non-initial stress both occur with high and low tone words.. (excepting the low back vowel /ɑ/ which occurs only in unstressed syllables)..…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Disyllables: stress on either syllable, initial more common, no discovered conditioning (possibly lexical); words of three or more syllables: penultimate stress (examples lo.ti.'di.yu 'satisfy', bu.'gyel.dang 'worm'). A reduced low back vowel is confined to unstressed syllables. Language is also tonal (high/low register word tone).
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the disyllabic variability itself; author notes few polysyllabic words in the database. Elsewhere (p. 223) compounds like chemendok 'egg' take initial stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in elicited citation forms; data chiefly from one Lukla (Pharak) speaker, corroborated by Khumbu speakers. Author explicitly flags the analysis as provisional.
new_statements.identity_note: Kelly 2004 describes Sherpa of the Solu-Khumbu district with primary data from a Lukla (Pharak) speaker and secondary Khumbu (Namche, Jamling) consultants = sher1255 proper. Watters 2002 and Gelu Sherpa 2008 describe the Solu (Phaplu) dialect, also sher1255. Graves 2007 (list of works to obtain) describes Hile Sherpa (Hile, eastern hills outside Solu-Khumbu), which Glottolog files under sher1255 but is a diaspora variety; check before merging.

new_statements.reading: First-hand fieldwork statement (Lukla/Khumbu consultants, with Solu comparison) on a tonal language: in disyllables stress is on the first or second syllable with no rule found (initial more common; possibly lexical), independent of tone; in the few longer words it is penultimate. Not on this search of works with stress in the title's item list but read in full during this search of works with stress in the title; it is the only explicit Sherpa word-stress placement statement located. It is not a fixed-stress description; a catalog's classification would have to be 'lexical/unpredictable in disyllables, penultimate in longer words' with a small database caveat.

sources.note: Section 2.9 'Stress', p. 219: in disyllables stress falls on the first or second syllable, initial more frequent; author could not work out a clear pattern, 'distribution may be lexically determined'; in polysyllabic (3+ syllable) words stress falls on the penultimate syllable (few such words); /a/-type low back vowel only in unstressed syllables. p. 223 uses word stress+tone as compound-hood evidence (mendok, chemendok initial stress). Data chiefly from a Lukla (Pharak) speaker with Khumbu secondary consultants.

sources.quote: Lhasa Tibetan and Sherpa (LTS) tone-l matches TGT initial K, LTS tone-2 matches TGT initial G, LTS intonation-1 matches TGT final K, LTS intonation-2 matches TGT final G. [...] Gordon has written the tones on these phrases (pg. 53) as high-high on "kiqki, high mid on 'teqki, low-mid on "tehki, and low-low on "dihki. The postposition -ki carries the second tone of the head word. The K syllable is in every case higher in pitch then a G syllable.
sources.locator: Part II pp. 1-8 (the scanned text); Sherpa section = paragraphs 7 and 9, Tables 6-11
sources.note: A comparative register/tone paper: proposes that the four 'prosodies' of Gurung/Tamang/Thakali and the two Lhasa-Tibetan-style tones plus two 'intonations' of Sherpa (from Kent Gordon's unpublished 'Sherpa Phonemic Summary', Part I pp. 45-60) reflect voiceless (K) vs voiced (G) initials of a disyllabic base. The Sherpa material is Gordon's pitch on noun + -ki phrases (high-high, high-mid, low-mid, low-low) and fortis/lenis, clear/breathy contrasts. Stress is mentioned only for Tamang ('three-tone, two-stress system'). No statement of where word stress falls in Sherpa.

sources.note: Silent on stress; consistent with the catalog source (Kelly 2004) in treating Sherpa as tonal (word-tone with four contours, cf. Pike & Schöttelndreyer 1973 fn. 2 already held by the project), but says nothing about stress placement, so it neither supports nor contradicts Kelly's 'first or second syllable, possibly lexical' statement. Identity: Sherpa of Solu-Khumbu (texts from Jangbu Sherpa, Ang Nyima Lama, Ang Gelbu Sherpa; SIL Solu work around Phaplu) = this languoid (sher1255).

sources.note: Sherpa (Solu dialect near Phaplu, one speaker) is classed as a 'word tone' language where one of four tones extends over the whole word incl. affixes (section 6.1.4, pp. 37-39); most words fall in pitch throughout; no statement on word-stress placement for Sherpa (stress remarks in the paper concern Lhomi/Dzongkha and Lhasa Tibetan).
